source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, however, an Apostle, concerning a persecutor, who first shed the Church's blood, afterwards changing the sword to a stylus, and converting the sword to a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, then himself bringing food according to Jacob, in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to himself! when rejoicing about the Thessalonians: So that, he says, we may glory in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures, which you endure, a demonstration of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as also to the Romans: Not only, however, but also rejoicing in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance truly testing, testing however hope, hope however does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, and heirs; heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ: if we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. For I consider the sufferings of this time not to be worthy of the glory, which will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what has been written: for Your sake we are killed all day, we have been considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own sufferings, he has predetermined that we must suffer: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. Which if they seem more inconveniences than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider it good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding words: Who in all things are troubled, but not constrained; and we are in need, but not in extreme need; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; who are cast down, but not perishing: always carrying the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is being destroyed, namely the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but the inner man is being renewed day by day; namely the soul by the hope of promises. For what is present, temporal and light, our pressure, through surpassing, surpassing into eternal weight of glory, is being perfected for us, not looking at what is seen, but at what is not seen. For what is seen is temporal, speaking about inconveniences; what is not seen, however, is eternal, promising about rewards. To the Thessalonians, however, writing about chains, he has affirmed that those are blessed, to whom it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having, he says, the same struggle, which you saw in me, and now hear. For even if I am poured out as a sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you rejoice and congratulate me in the same way. You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, by which he acquires solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become next to his own wish, he writes to Timothy, exulting about his own prospect? For I am already being poured out, and the time of departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely of passion. It is sufficient that he has spoken above: Faithful is the word: if we have died with Christ, and we live; if we suffer, and we will reign; if we deny, and He will deny us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. So do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me, bound by Him; because He has foretold: For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, and love, and a sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence. But also where he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than for martyrdoms? where he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?

pass_b_english: Paul the Apostle began as a persecutor who first shed the Church's blood; afterwards he exchanged the sword for a stylus and turned the blade into a plow. Once a ravenous wolf of Benjamin, he then brought food himself, in line with Jacob's prophecy, and in that very role he commends martyrdoms—now even desirable to himself. Rejoicing over the Thessalonians, he writes: "So that we may boast about you in the churches of God for your endurance and faith in all the persecutions and pressures you endure" (2 Thessalonians 1:4). These sufferings are evidence of God's just judgment, so that you may be counted worthy of his kingdom, for which you also suffer.

To the Romans he says the same: "Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces endurance; endurance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not put us to shame" (Romans 5:3–5). And again: "If we are children, then we are heirs—heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him" (Romans 8:17). "I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us" (Romans 8:18).

And therefore afterwards: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or hardship or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? As it is written: 'For your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.' No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:35, 38–39).

To the Corinthians, enumerating his own sufferings, he insists that suffering is necessary: "I have worked much harder, been in prison more frequently, been flogged more severely, and been exposed to death again and again. Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned" (2 Corinthians 11:23–25). If these seem more like hardships than martyrdoms, he adds: "That is why, for Christ's sake, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties" (2 Corinthians 12:10).

Earlier he wrote: "We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed. We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus" (2 Corinthians 4:8–10). "Though outwardly we are wasting away, yet inwardly we are being renewed day by day. For our light and momentary troubles are achieving for us an eternal glory that far outweighs them all. So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal" (2 Corinthians 4:16–18).

Writing to the Thessalonians about his chains, he declares blessed those to whom it has been given not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him: "You are going through the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have" (Philippians 1:30). "Even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service coming from your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you. So you too should be glad and rejoice with me" (Philippians 2:17–18). You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, which gains its solemnity from mutual joy.

So that, having reached the very thing he wished for, he writes to Timothy exulting over his prospect? "For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time for my departure is near. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Now there is in store for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day" (2 Timothy 4:7–8). It is enough that he has spoken above: "Here is a trustworthy saying: If we died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him. If we disown him, he will also disown us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself" (2 Timothy 2:11–13).

Therefore do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; because he foretold: "For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-discipline" (2 Timothy 1:7–8). We suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, because we suffer for innocence. But also, when he commands endurance, for whom does he foresee it more than for martyrs? When he tears people away from idolatry, what does he tear them away with more than martyrdoms?

review.notes: Pass B violates the rule against adding to the text (Pass A/Latin) by inserting extensive content not present in the source. Specifically, in the section corresponding to Romans 8:35-39, Pass B adds 'neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, nor anything else in all creation', which is not in the Locked Latin 'neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio'. Similarly, in the section for 2 Timothy 4:7-8, Pass B adds 'of righteousness' and 'the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me', which are not in the Locked Latin 'superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet'. These are expansions into biblical wording rather than translations of the provided Latin text.
reasons: Pass B adds content not present in the Locked Latin: 'neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, nor anything else in all creation' (for 'neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio') and 'of righteousness' / 'the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me' (for 'superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet').
